resources.title: Periodic table
resources.summary: An interactive periodic table, following the one AQA prints in every Chemistry exam. Press any element for its atomic number, relative atomic mass and what those tell you; press a family to pick it out.
resources.statusNote: AQA prints the table in every paper. It gives each element's symbol, name, atomic number and relative atomic mass, rounded to whole numbers except copper (63.5) and chlorine (35.5). It does **not** give ion charges or the reactivity series: those you learn.

sources.name: AQA GCSE Chemistry specification (8462)
sources.where: Section 9, Appendix A (an older printing: elements 113, 115, 117 and 118 carry temporary names)

applications.title: Predicting before testing
applications.body: Mendeleev left gaps in his table for elements nobody had found, and predicted their properties from their neighbours. Gallium and germanium were found later and matched.

applications.title: Choosing materials
applications.body: Engineers who need a light, strong metal look along Groups 2 and 3 and the lighter transition metals, which is why aircraft use aluminium and titanium alloys.

applications.title: Working out a formula
applications.body: Sodium is in Group 1 and forms Na⁺; chlorine in Group 7 forms Cl⁻. The group alone tells you that table salt is NaCl.

blocks.alt: An interactive periodic table of the 90 elements on the AQA insert, coloured by family, with a panel that shows the pressed element's symbol, name, atomic number, relative atomic mass and family, and under it how to read them: the element's neutrons worked out, and what its row and column say, with buttons that pick the row or column out of the table

resources.title: Common ions
resources.summary: The charges on the ions you meet in the course, positive and negative, including the ions made of more than one atom, and how to use them to write the formula of a compound.

applications.title: Reading a water bottle label
applications.body: The minerals listed on bottled water, calcium Ca²⁺, magnesium Mg²⁺, sodium Na⁺, chloride Cl⁻ and sulfate SO₄²⁻, are these ions, measured in milligrams per litre.

applications.title: Fertilisers
applications.body: A bag of fertiliser lists ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃: one ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, for every nitrate, NO₃⁻, because their charges cancel one for one.

blocks.title: Positive ions
rows: hydrogen $\text{H}^{+}$, lithium $\text{Li}^{+}$, sodium $\text{Na}^{+}$, potassium $\text{K}^{+}$, silver $\text{Ag}^{+}$, ammonium $\text{NH}_4^{+}$
magnesium $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, calcium $\text{Ca}^{2+}$, barium $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, copper(II) $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, iron(II) $\text{Fe}^{2+}$, zinc $\text{Zn}^{2+}$
blocks.note: Metals form positive ions. So do hydrogen and ammonium, which are not metals. A Roman numeral in a name gives the charge where a metal can have more than one: iron(II) is $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and iron(III) is $\text{Fe}^{3+}$.

blocks.title: Negative ions
blocks.note: Non-metals form negative ions. Hydroxide, nitrate, sulfate and carbonate are each made of more than one atom, and the charge belongs to the whole group.

blocks.body:
**What an ion is.** An atom, or a group of atoms, with a charge, because it has lost or gained electrons. Losing electrons leaves a positive ion. Gaining them makes a negative ion.

**From the group.** Atoms in Group 1 lose one electron, so they form $1+$ ions. Group 2 lose two: $2+$. Group 7 gain one: $1-$. Group 6 gain two: $2-$. The other charges in the tables cannot be read from the group in this way. Learn them: silver $1+$, zinc $2+$, aluminium $3+$, copper(II), iron(II), iron(III), and the ions made of more than one atom.

**Writing a formula.** The charges must add up to zero. Write the two ions, then find how many of each make the charges cancel.

- **Sodium chloride.** $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$: $+1$ and $-1$ cancel one for one, so $\text{NaCl}$.
- **Magnesium chloride.** $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$: one magnesium ion gives $+2$, so it needs two chloride ions, $-2$. The formula is $\text{MgCl}_2$.
- **Calcium hydroxide.** $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$: one calcium ion needs two hydroxide ions. Hydroxide is made of two atoms, so it goes in a bracket: $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$.
- **Aluminium sulfate.** $\text{Al}^{3+}$ and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$: two aluminium ions give $+6$ and three sulfate ions give $-6$, so $\text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3$.

A bracket goes round an ion made of more than one atom, and only when the formula needs more than one of that ion. The charges are not written in the finished formula.

resources.title: Reactivity series
resources.summary: The metals the specification names, most reactive first, with carbon and hydrogen placed among them, how each reacts with water and dilute acid at room temperature, and what the order decides.

blocks.title: Most reactive at the top
rows: reacts violently: fizzes, melts, and the hydrogen burns lilac
reacts vigorously: fizzes and melts into a ball that skims about
barely: a few bubbles over days
*not a metal: placed here as a marker*
*not a metal: see the note for what the marker shows*
*not a metal: placed here as a marker*
*not a metal: see the note for what the marker shows*
blocks.note: Carbon and hydrogen are non-metals. They are in the list as markers. A metal below carbon can be extracted from its oxide by heating with carbon. A metal below hydrogen does not react with dilute acid. All reactions are at room temperature: the specification does not include reactions with steam. A metal that reacts gives off hydrogen, and the faster the fizzing, the more reactive the metal.

blocks.body:
**What the order decides.**

- **Displacement.** A more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive one in a compound. To predict it, find both metals in the list. If the metal you add is higher than the metal in the compound, it displaces it. Zinc is above copper, so zinc in copper sulfate solution gives zinc sulfate and a coating of copper. Copper is below zinc, so copper in zinc sulfate solution does nothing.
- **Extraction.** Metals below carbon, such as zinc, iron and copper, can be extracted by heating their oxides with carbon. The carbon takes the oxygen. Metals above carbon, such as sodium and aluminium, are too reactive for that. They are extracted by electrolysis: the compound is melted and split with an electric current. Aluminium is not one of the eight metals to learn in order. It sits between magnesium and carbon.
- **Why the order.** A reactive metal loses its outer electrons easily to form a positive ion. Going up the series, that happens more readily.

**A mnemonic.** *Please Send Lions, Cats, Monkeys, Cute Zebras Into Hot Countries*: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, carbon, zinc, iron, hydrogen, copper. Three words start with C. They stand for calcium, carbon and copper, in that order.

applications.title: Why gold is found as gold
applications.body: Gold is so unreactive that it sits below copper and is found in the ground as the metal itself, while sodium, near the top, is only ever found in compounds.

applications.title: Protecting a ship
applications.body: Blocks of zinc bolted to a steel hull corrode instead of the iron in the steel, because zinc is more reactive. This is called sacrificial protection. Galvanising, which coats iron with zinc, works the same way.

resources.title: Chemical tests
resources.summary: The tests for gases and for ions that the specification lists, each with the result it gives: the four gases, flame colours, the metal hydroxide precipitates, and the tests for carbonates, halides and sulfates.

blocks.title: Gases
rows: a burning splint at the mouth of the tube
a glowing splint in the tube
blocks.note: Limewater is a solution of calcium hydroxide in water.

blocks.title: Flame tests (Chemistry only)
blocks.note: Dip a clean wire loop in the sample and hold it in a blue Bunsen flame. In a mixture, one colour can hide another: the strong yellow of sodium masks the rest.

blocks.title: Add sodium hydroxide solution (Chemistry only)
blocks.note: A precipitate is a solid that forms when two solutions are mixed. It turns the liquid cloudy. Add a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution, then keep adding: that is adding it in excess. Only aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess, which tells it apart from calcium and magnesium. To tell calcium from magnesium, use a flame test: calcium gives orange-red.

blocks.title: Negative ions (Chemistry only)
rows: add dilute acid, bubble the gas through limewater
add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution
add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution
add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution
add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution

blocks.body: **Putting tests together.** An unknown salt gives a lilac flame, so it contains potassium ions, $\text{K}^{+}$. With dilute hydrochloric acid and barium chloride solution it gives a white precipitate, so it contains sulfate ions, $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$. The salt is potassium sulfate, $\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4$.

applications.title: Fireworks
applications.body: A firework's colours are flame colours. Strontium or lithium salts burn red, calcium salts orange and sodium salts yellow. Makers mix salts to get the colours between.

applications.title: Testing tap water
applications.body: Water companies check tap water for ions such as chloride and sulfate. They use instruments, which are faster and more accurate than test-tube tests and can find much smaller amounts.

resources.title: pH scale and indicators
resources.summary: The pH scale from 0 to 14 in the colours universal indicator turns, with everyday substances placed on it, how pH is measured and, for Higher tier, what a change of one pH unit means.

visual.alt: The pH scale from 0 to 14 as a bar coloured red through orange, yellow, green, blue and purple, with stomach acid, lemon juice, vinegar, pure water, baking soda solution, soap and oven cleaner listed with their pH values and colours

blocks.body:
**Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline.** Acids release hydrogen ions, $\text{H}^{+}$, in water. Alkalis release hydroxide ions, $\text{OH}^{-}$. A base is a substance that neutralises an acid, and an alkali is a base that dissolves in water. In neutralisation the two ions make water: $\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + \text{OH}^{-}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$.

**Measuring pH.** Universal indicator is a mixture of dyes. Add a few drops, or dip indicator paper, and match the colour to the chart. It gives an approximate pH. A pH probe gives a reading on a meter instead.

**Higher tier.** Each fall of one pH unit means ten times the concentration of hydrogen ions. A solution of pH 2 has ten times the hydrogen ion concentration of one at pH 3, and a hundred times that of one at pH 4.

applications.title: Swimming pools
applications.body: Pool water is kept at about pH 7.2 to 7.6. Any lower and it stings the eyes; any higher and the chlorine that keeps it clean stops working well.

applications.title: Soil and gardening
applications.body: Farmers test soil pH and spread lime, a base, on acidic fields, because most crops grow best near neutral.

applications.title: Indigestion tablets
applications.body: They contain a base such as calcium carbonate that neutralises excess stomach acid, raising its pH.

resources.title: How bonds form
resources.summary: What the electrons do in each kind of bond: given away in an ionic bond, shared in a covalent one, set free in a metal. How to draw a dot-and-cross diagram, step by step, and all eight molecules the course asks you to draw.

applications.title: Salt on your chips
applications.body: Table salt formed when sodium atoms each gave one electron to a chlorine atom. Sodium is a soft metal that fizzes in water and chlorine a poisonous gas, yet sodium chloride is safe to eat, because its ions behave nothing like the atoms they came from.

applications.title: A gas hob
applications.body: A gas hob burns methane, $\text{CH}_4$. Its four covalent C–H bonds break, and the new bonds made in carbon dioxide and water give out more energy than breaking the old ones took in. The difference is the heat that cooks the food.

applications.title: Copper wire
applications.body: Copper carries the current in household wiring because of its metallic bonds: the outer electrons of every copper atom are free to move through the whole wire, so they can flow along it.

blocks.title: Three kinds of strong bond
rows: the metal atom gives its outer electrons to the non-metal atom; both become ions with a full outer shell, and the opposite charges attract
two atoms each put one electron into a pair they share; each shared pair is one bond
every atom’s outer electrons leave it and move through the whole piece; the positive ions left behind are held by this sea of electrons
blocks.note: Atoms bond to reach a full outer shell, like the noble gases in Group 0: eight electrons, or two for hydrogen. An ion is an atom that has lost or gained electrons, so it has a charge.

blocks.body:
**Drawing an ionic dot-and-cross diagram.**

1. Find each atom’s outer electrons from its group: sodium, Group 1, has one; chlorine, Group 7, has seven.
2. Move the metal’s outer electrons onto the non-metal. Draw the metal’s electrons as crosses and the non-metal’s as dots, so you can see which came from where.
3. Draw each ion in square brackets with its charge at the top right: a Group 1 metal loses one electron and becomes $1+$, Group 2 becomes $2+$; a Group 7 non-metal gains one and becomes $1-$, Group 6 becomes $2-$.
4. Check that the charges add up to zero. If not, add another ion: magnesium gives two electrons but chlorine takes only one, so magnesium chloride needs two chloride ions, $\text{MgCl}_2$.

The course asks for metals in Groups 1 and 2 with non-metals in Groups 6 and 7.

visual.alt: A dot-and-cross diagram for sodium chloride: sodium’s one outer electron moves to chlorine, leaving a sodium ion with charge 1+ and a chloride ion with charge 1− and eight outer electrons
A dot-and-cross diagram for magnesium oxide: magnesium’s two outer electrons move to oxygen, leaving a magnesium ion with charge 2+ and an oxide ion with charge 2− and eight outer electrons

blocks.body:
**Drawing a covalent dot-and-cross diagram.**

1. Find each atom’s outer electrons from its group.
2. Work out how many more each atom needs for a full shell. That is how many bonds it makes (table below).
3. Overlap the outer shells and put the shared pairs in the overlap: one electron from each atom in every pair, a dot and a cross.
4. Draw the rest of each atom’s outer electrons in pairs outside the overlap. Check every atom now has eight, or two for hydrogen.

A line is the short way to draw a shared pair: one line for a single bond, two for a double, three for a triple.

blocks.title: Bonds each atom makes
blocks.note: Bonds made = electrons needed to reach eight, or two for hydrogen. Chlorine stands for Group 7, oxygen for Group 6, nitrogen for Group 5, carbon for Group 4.

blocks.title: The eight molecules to draw
blocks.note: AQA names these eight in 4.2.1.4. Shared and unshared pairs together hold every outer electron: water has $6 + 1 + 1 = 8$, which is 2 shared pairs and 2 pairs left on the oxygen. Carbon dioxide, $\text{O=C=O}$, is not on the list, but it has two double bonds.

visual.alt: A dot-and-cross diagram of a hydrogen molecule, H2: two hydrogen atoms share one pair of electrons, one electron from each atom

blocks.caption: **Hydrogen, $\text{H}_2$.** One shared pair: each atom now has two electrons, a full first shell.

visual.alt: A dot-and-cross diagram of a chlorine molecule, Cl2: two chlorine atoms share one pair, and each keeps three pairs of its own

blocks.caption: **Chlorine, $\text{Cl}_2$.** One shared pair; each atom keeps three pairs of its own, so both have eight.

visual.alt: A dot-and-cross diagram of hydrogen chloride: hydrogen and chlorine share one pair of electrons, and chlorine keeps three pairs of its own

blocks.caption: **Hydrogen chloride, $\text{HCl}$.** One shared pair: hydrogen has two electrons, chlorine eight.

visual.alt: A dot-and-cross diagram of an oxygen molecule, O2: two oxygen atoms share two pairs of electrons, a double bond, and each keeps two pairs of its own

blocks.caption: **Oxygen, $\text{O}_2$.** Two shared pairs, a double bond: each oxygen needs two more electrons.

visual.alt: A dot-and-cross diagram of a nitrogen molecule, N2: the two nitrogen atoms share three pairs of electrons, a triple bond, and each keeps one pair of its own

blocks.caption: **Nitrogen, $\text{N}_2$.** Three shared pairs, a triple bond: each nitrogen needs three more.

visual.alt: A dot-and-cross diagram of water: an oxygen atom shares one pair with each of two hydrogen atoms and keeps two pairs of its own

blocks.caption: **Water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.** Oxygen shares a pair with each hydrogen and keeps two pairs of its own.

visual.alt: A dot-and-cross diagram of ammonia: a nitrogen atom shares one pair with each of three hydrogen atoms and keeps one pair of its own

blocks.caption: **Ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$.** Nitrogen shares a pair with each of three hydrogens and keeps one pair of its own.

visual.alt: A dot-and-cross diagram of methane: a carbon atom shares one pair with each of four hydrogen atoms, using all four of its outer electrons

blocks.caption: **Methane, $\text{CH}_4$.** Carbon shares a pair with each of four hydrogens, using all four outer electrons.

blocks.body:
**Metallic bonding.** There is no diagram to draw atom by atom. The outer electrons of every metal atom are delocalised: free to move through the whole structure. What is left is a regular pattern of positive ions in a sea of electrons, and the attraction between them is the metallic bond. The Structures and bonding sheet draws it.

**What a dot-and-cross diagram cannot show.** It shows where the electrons go, but not the shape of a molecule, and for an ionic compound it shows one pair of ions, not the giant lattice they build. The electrons are all the same; dots and crosses only mark where each one came from.

**How to remember it.**

- **Bonds each atom makes: HONC 1234.** Hydrogen 1, Oxygen 2, Nitrogen 3, Carbon 4. Check any molecule against it: in water, oxygen has two bonds and each hydrogen one.
- **Ion charges from the group.** A metal’s charge is its group number, positive: Group 2 gives $2+$. A non-metal’s is 8 minus its group, negative: Group 6 gives $2-$.
- **Draw, don’t read.** Close the page and draw each of the eight molecules from memory, then check the shared pairs against the table. The ones you get wrong are the ones to draw again tomorrow.

resources.title: Structures and bonding
resources.summary: The four kinds of structure side by side: ionic, simple molecular, giant covalent and metallic, each drawn, with what holds it together and the properties that follow.

blocks.title: Structure decides properties
rows: strong attraction between oppositely charged ions, in every direction
when melted or dissolved, as the ions can move
strong covalent bonds inside each molecule; weak forces between molecules
no: the molecules have no overall charge
no, except graphite, which has delocalised electrons
positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons
yes, as the delocalised electrons move
blocks.note: Giant means the pattern repeats through the whole piece, with no separate molecules. A lattice is a regular, repeating arrangement. Delocalised electrons are outer electrons that are free to move through the whole structure, so they can carry charge.

blocks.body: **Working backwards.** A white solid melts at 801 °C. It does not conduct electricity as a solid, but it does when melted. The high melting point rules out simple molecular. Conducting only when melted means charged particles that are fixed in the solid and free in the liquid: ions. The structure is ionic. This one is sodium chloride.

visual.alt: A giant ionic lattice: alternating positive and negative ions in a regular grid

blocks.caption: **Ionic.** A giant lattice of positive and negative ions.

visual.alt: Simple molecules: pairs of atoms strongly bonded, scattered with weak forces between the molecules

blocks.caption: **Simple molecular.** Small molecules, drawn here as pairs of atoms such as oxygen. The bonds inside each molecule are strong. The forces between molecules are weak, so little energy separates them.

visual.alt: A giant covalent lattice such as diamond: every atom bonded to its neighbours

blocks.caption: **Giant covalent: diamond.** In diamond every carbon atom is bonded to four others, in three dimensions. This flat sketch shows a small piece, so the atoms at its edges are drawn with fewer bonds. In the real structure the pattern carries on.

visual.alt: Graphite: two layers of hexagons with weak forces between the layers

blocks.caption: **Giant covalent: graphite.** Layers of joined hexagons. Each carbon is bonded to three others in its layer, and one electron from each carbon is delocalised. There are no covalent bonds between the layers.

visual.alt: Metallic structure: rows of positive ions with delocalised electrons between them

blocks.caption: **Metallic.** Positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.

applications.title: Pencils
applications.body: A pencil writes because graphite's layers slide off onto the paper: the forces between layers are weak, though every layer is held together by strong covalent bonds.

applications.title: Gritting roads
applications.body: Salt is ionic, so it does not melt in winter; it dissolves in the water on the road instead, and the salty solution freezes at a lower temperature.

resources.title: Naming compounds
resources.summary: How a compound’s name is built and what its ending tells you: ‑ide, ‑ate and ‑ite, the Roman numerals and the older ‑ous and ‑ic, the salts each acid makes, and the prefixes mono-, di- and tri-. With a chart that names a compound from its formula, and ways to remember the rules.

applications.title: Iron tablets
applications.body: A packet of iron tablets may say ferrous sulfate. That is the older name for iron(II) sulfate, $\text{FeSO}_4$: ‑ous marks the lower of iron’s two charges, $\text{Fe}^{2+}$.

applications.title: Wine and bacon labels
applications.body: Wine labels say “contains sulphites”, and bacon lists sodium nitrite, $\text{NaNO}_2$, as a preservative. Both are ‑ite ions: one oxygen fewer than sulfate and nitrate.

applications.title: Laughing gas
applications.body: The gas a dentist or a midwife gives for pain is nitrous oxide, $\text{N}_2\text{O}$. Its systematic name, dinitrogen monoxide, counts the atoms with prefixes: two nitrogens, one oxygen.

blocks.body: **A name has two halves.** An ionic compound is named positive ion first, then negative ion: sodium chloride, copper(II) sulfate. The metal keeps its own name. The non-metal part changes its ending, and the ending tells you what is in it. The formula is written in the same order: metal first.

nodes.text: Can the metal have two charges?

visual.alt: A flow chart for naming an ionic compound from its formula: name the metal or ammonium; if the metal can have two charges add (II) or (III); if there is just one other element its name ends ‑ide; if the rest is OH it is hydroxide; if the rest is sulfate, nitrate or carbonate it ends ‑ate; if it has one oxygen fewer it ends ‑ite; then write the metal first and the ion second

blocks.caption: **From formula to name.** Ask the questions in order. $\text{FeCl}_3$: iron can be $2+$ or $3+$, and three $\text{Cl}^{-}$ make $3-$, so iron(III); then just chlorine, so chloride: iron(III) chloride.

blocks.title: Endings, and when each is used
rows: the non-metal on its own: the compound has just two elements
sodium chloride, $\text{NaCl}$; magnesium oxide, $\text{MgO}$; zinc sulfide, $\text{ZnS}$
the non-metal joined to oxygen, in the ion with more oxygen
sulfate $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$, nitrate $\text{NO}_3^{-}$, carbonate $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, phosphate $\text{PO}_4^{3-}$: copper(II) sulfate, $\text{CuSO}_4$
the same non-metal and oxygen with one oxygen fewer than the ‑ate, and the same charge
a positive ion made of non-metals
breaks the ‑ide rule: two elements in the ion, oxygen and hydrogen
a metal that can form more than one ion; the numeral is its charge
the same two charges in older names: ‑ous the lower, ‑ic the higher, often on the Latin name
ferrous $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is iron(II), ferric $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is iron(III); cuprous $\text{Cu}^{+}$ is copper(I), cupric $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is copper(II)
blocks.note: AQA writes names with ‑ide, ‑ate, ‑ium and Roman numerals, and those are what the exam uses. The ‑ite ions and the ‑ous and ‑ic names are not on the course, but they are on food labels, medicine packets and in older books, so it helps to read them.

blocks.title: Each acid names its salts
blocks.note: A salt keeps the acid’s negative ion and swaps its hydrogen for a metal. The pattern: a hydro-…‑ic acid makes ‑ide salts, an ‑ic acid makes ‑ate salts, an ‑ous acid makes ‑ite salts.

blocks.title: Prefixes: compounds of two non-metals
blocks.note: Two non-metals make a covalent compound, with no charges to balance, so the name counts the atoms instead. Mono- is left off the first element: $\text{CO}$ is carbon monoxide, not monocarbon monoxide. Where two vowels meet, one is dropped: monoxide, not monooxide.

blocks.body:
**How to remember it.**

- **Acids and their salts:** “I **ate** something **ic**ky, and the b**ite** was danger**ous**.” An ‑ic acid makes ‑ate salts; an ‑ous acid makes ‑ite salts.
- **‑ate or ‑ite:** ‑ate has more oxygen. Think of the ion that **ate** an extra oxygen.
- **‑ous or ‑ic:** h**i**gh has an i, like -**i**c; l**o**w has an o, like -**o**us. Ferric is the higher charge, $\text{Fe}^{3+}$.
- **Practise both ways.** Cover the name and say it from the formula, then cover the formula and write it from the name. Ten minutes on three different days fixes it better than thirty minutes once.

resources.title: Common compounds
resources.summary: The compounds the course keeps naming, each with its formula, its structure and how it is made: the reaction that makes it, or where it is found. Grouped as acids, alkalis, salts, precipitates, oxides and carbon compounds, to cover and learn.

applications.title: The kitchen cupboard
applications.body: Table salt is sodium chloride, $\text{NaCl}$, and vinegar is a dilute solution of ethanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$. The limescale inside a kettle is calcium carbonate, $\text{CaCO}_3$: an acid descaler fizzes it away as carbon dioxide.

applications.title: Making cement
applications.body: Cement starts with limestone, calcium carbonate, heated in a kiln. It breaks down to calcium oxide and carbon dioxide, which is one reason cement works are among the largest industrial sources of carbon dioxide.

applications.title: A barium meal
applications.body: Before an X-ray of the gut, a patient drinks barium sulfate, $\text{BaSO}_4$, the white precipitate of the sulfate test. It does not dissolve, so the body does not absorb it, and it blocks X-rays, so the gut shows up white.

blocks.body:
**How to learn it.** Learn one table at a time. Cover the Formula column and write each formula from the name, then check it from the charges on the Common ions sheet: the charges must cancel. Next day, cover the name and say it from the formula. The Naming compounds sheet gives the rules behind every name, so most formulae can be worked out rather than learnt.

**Elements that come in pairs.** Not compounds, but written the same way in every equation: hydrogen $\text{H}_2$, nitrogen $\text{N}_2$, oxygen $\text{O}_2$, and the halogens fluorine $\text{F}_2$, chlorine $\text{Cl}_2$, bromine $\text{Br}_2$ and iodine $\text{I}_2$. Each is a molecule of two atoms.

**What the structure column means.** Ionic: a giant lattice of ions, from a metal (or ammonium) with a non-metal. Small molecules: non-metal atoms sharing electrons in separate molecules. Giant covalent: shared bonds through the whole piece. The Structures and bonding sheet shows each one.

blocks.title: Acids
rows: Hydrogen chloride gas dissolved in water. The gas forms when hydrogen burns in chlorine: $\text{H}_2 + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{HCl}$.

Made in industry from sulfur, which is burnt and oxidised to sulfur trioxide; the last step is $\text{SO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$. The steps before it are not on the AQA course.
Made in industry from ammonia, which is oxidised and the gas dissolved in water. The course says only that ammonia is used to make it.
Ethanol oxidised, by an oxidising agent or by microbes with air: wine left open turns to vinegar. $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.
blocks.note: Every acid makes hydrogen ions, $\text{H}^{+}$, in water. The rest of the formula names the salts it makes: hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, sulfuric acid sulfates, nitric acid nitrates.

blocks.title: Alkalis and bases
rows: Sodium with water: $2\text{Na} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2$. In industry, from the electrolysis of sodium chloride solution (brine), which also gives hydrogen and chlorine.
Potassium with water, faster and with a lilac flame: $2\text{K} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{KOH} + \text{H}_2$.
Calcium oxide with water: $\text{CaO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2$. Its solution is limewater, the test for carbon dioxide.
The Haber process: $\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3$ over an iron catalyst at about 450 °C and 200 atmospheres. Nitrogen comes from the air and hydrogen from natural gas.
blocks.note: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water, giving hydroxide ions, $\text{OH}^{-}$. A base neutralises an acid to make a salt and water.

blocks.title: Salts
rows: Mined as rock salt, or left when sea water evaporates. Sodium burns in chlorine to make it: $2\text{Na} + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NaCl}$. Neutralising gives it too: $\text{NaOH} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Copper(II) oxide added to warm sulfuric acid until no more reacts, filtered, then crystallised (Required practical 1): $\text{CuO} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{CuSO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Magnesium with hydrochloric acid, fizzing out hydrogen: $\text{Mg} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2 + \text{H}_2$.
Marble chips (calcium carbonate) with hydrochloric acid, the reaction used to measure rates: $\text{CaCO}_3 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$.
Found as limestone, chalk and marble. It forms when carbon dioxide turns limewater milky: $\text{Ca(OH)}_2 + \text{CO}_2 \rightarrow \text{CaCO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Potassium hydroxide neutralised by nitric acid: $\text{KOH} + \text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{KNO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. A fertiliser, giving plants potassium and nitrogen.
Ammonia neutralised by nitric acid: $\text{NH}_3 + \text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$. A fertiliser rich in nitrogen.
Ammonia neutralised by sulfuric acid, in a lab by titration: $2\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{(NH}_4\text{)}_2\text{SO}_4$.
blocks.note: A salt is the compound left when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal or by ammonium. Its first name comes from the metal, its second from the acid. The ammonium, nitrate and sulfate ions are held together inside by covalent bonds, but the salts are ionic: the ions attract one another.

blocks.title: Precipitates from the ion tests
rows: White precipitate: silver nitrate solution, with dilute nitric acid, added to a chloride: $\text{AgNO}_3 + \text{NaCl} \rightarrow \text{AgCl} + \text{NaNO}_3$. A bromide gives cream silver bromide, an iodide yellow silver iodide.
White precipitate: barium chloride solution, with dilute hydrochloric acid, added to a sulfate: $\text{BaCl}_2 + \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4 + 2\text{NaCl}$.
Blue precipitate: sodium hydroxide solution added to a copper(II) salt: $\text{CuSO}_4 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Cu(OH)}_2 + \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$.
Green precipitate: sodium hydroxide solution added to an iron(II) salt: $\text{FeSO}_4 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Fe(OH)}_2 + \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$.
Brown precipitate: sodium hydroxide solution added to an iron(III) salt: $\text{FeCl}_3 + 3\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Fe(OH)}_3 + 3\text{NaCl}$.
blocks.note: A precipitate is a solid that forms when two solutions are mixed, because one product does not dissolve. Its colour tells you which ion was there.

blocks.title: Oxides
rows: Hydrogen reacts with oxygen, burning in a rocket engine or without a flame in a fuel cell: $2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Any fuel that contains hydrogen makes water when it burns.
Carbon burning with plenty of oxygen: $\text{C} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2$. Also from any acid with a carbonate, and from heating a carbonate.
Carbon burning with too little oxygen (incomplete combustion): $2\text{C} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CO}$. A toxic gas with no colour or smell.
Sulfur in a fuel burning: $\text{S} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{SO}_2$. It dissolves in rain and makes acid rain.
Nitrogen and oxygen from the air react in the heat of an engine: $\text{N}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{NO}$. In the air it reacts on to nitrogen dioxide, $\text{NO}_2$.
Magnesium burning with a bright white flame: $2\text{Mg} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MgO}$.
Limestone heated until it breaks down (thermal decomposition): $\text{CaCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2$.
Copper heated in air, turning black: $2\text{Cu} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CuO}$.
Found as iron ore. Iron reacts with oxygen: $4\text{Fe} + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$. Rust is this oxide with water in it, which is why iron needs both air and water to rust.
Found as the ore bauxite, and electrolysed to extract aluminium. In air a thin layer forms on aluminium and stops it corroding further: $4\text{Al} + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$.
Found as sand and quartz. Not made in the course.
blocks.note: An oxide is an element joined to oxygen. A metal oxide is ionic and is a base; a non-metal oxide is made of small molecules, and many of them make acids in water.

blocks.title: Carbon compounds
rows: Most of natural gas. The fuel in a gas cooker.
Separated from crude oil and natural gas, in the gas fraction.
Separated from crude oil in the gas fraction; sold in bottles for camping stoves and barbecues.
Separated from crude oil in the gas fraction; the fuel in a lighter.
Cracking a longer alkane over a hot catalyst or with steam, for example: $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{22} \rightarrow \text{C}_8\text{H}_{18} + \text{C}_2\text{H}_4$.

Fermentation: yeast turns sugar into ethanol at 25–35 °C with no oxygen: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 \rightarrow 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 2\text{CO}_2$. Or ethene with steam over a catalyst: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$.

Ethanoic acid and ethanol warmed with an acid catalyst: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. An ester, with a fruity smell; used as a solvent.
Many ethene molecules join in addition polymerisation: $n\,\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 \rightarrow \text{(C}_2\text{H}_4\text{)}_n$. The plastic of carrier bags.
blocks.note: Most of these come from crude oil, a mixture of hydrocarbons (compounds of hydrogen and carbon only) separated by fractional distillation.

resources.title: Homologous series
resources.summary: The four families of organic compounds in the course: alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids, with their functional groups and first four members, and two of each family drawn in full.

blocks.body:
**What a homologous series is.** A family of compounds that share a functional group and a general formula. Each member has one more carbon atom than the one before. The functional group is the part of the molecule that reacts, so members of a family react in the same way.

**Using a general formula.** Put the number of carbons in place of $n$. Propane has three carbons, so the alkane formula $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$ gives $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8$. Propene also has three, so the alkene formula $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}$ gives $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$.

blocks.title: Four families
rows: none: every bond is a single bond
methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acid
blocks.note: The name tells you the carbons: *meth-* one, *eth-* two, *prop-* three, *but-* four, *pent-* five. The ending tells you the family: *-ane*, *-ene*, *-ol*, *-oic acid*. The alkenes start at ethene, because a double bond between carbons needs two carbons.

visual.alt: The displayed formulae of ethane and ethene side by side, showing that ethene has a double bond between its two carbons and two fewer hydrogen atoms

props.title: Two fewer hydrogens, and a second bond in their place

blocks.caption: **Alkane and alkene.** Ethane is saturated: every bond is single, so it holds as many hydrogens as it can. Ethene is unsaturated: its double bond takes the place of two hydrogens.

visual.alt: The displayed formulae of methanol and ethanol, each showing the oxygen hydrogen group drawn as an O joined to an H at the end of the carbon chain

props.title: Every bond drawn, including the O-H

blocks.caption: **Alcohols.** The –OH group on the end carbon.

visual.alt: The displayed formulae of methanoic acid and ethanoic acid, each showing the carboxyl group with one oxygen double bonded to the carbon and the other joined to a hydrogen

props.title: One carbon, two oxygens: the -COOH group

blocks.caption: **Carboxylic acids.** The –COOH group: one oxygen double bonded, one with a hydrogen.

applications.title: Fuels
applications.body: Methane is natural gas. Propane and butane fill camping gas canisters. Petrol is a mixture of larger hydrocarbons, mostly alkanes. With plenty of air, all of them burn to carbon dioxide and water.

applications.title: Vinegar and hand gel
applications.body: Vinegar is a dilute solution of ethanoic acid, a carboxylic acid; hand sanitiser is mostly ethanol, an alcohol.

resources.title: Required practicals
resources.summary: The eight required practicals in AQA Chemistry: what each investigates and what you measure. Two, titration and identifying ions, are Chemistry only.

blocks.title: The eight required practicals
rows: add an insoluble oxide or carbonate to hot dilute acid until no more reacts, filter off what is left, warm the solution until crystals start to form, then leave it to crystallise
a pure, dry sample of the salt
measure 25 cm³ of alkali into a flask with a pipette, add indicator, then run in acid from a burette until the colour changes
the reacting volumes; at Higher tier, a concentration in mol/dm³ and g/dm³
pass an electric current through salt solutions, using electrodes that do not react, such as carbon rods
react solutions such as acid and metal, or acid and alkali
the temperature change, and what affects it
run a reaction at different concentrations, by two methods
the volume of gas given off over time, and the time for a solution to turn cloudy
the $R_f$ value of each spot: the distance the spot moved divided by the distance the solvent moved
run the flame, hydroxide, carbonate, halide and sulfate tests
which ions an unknown compound holds
test samples from different sources, and distil one
the pH and dissolved solids, and pure water
blocks.note: AQA says questions drawing on the practicals count for at least 15% of the marks. Know the method, the variables and the hazards of each. An $R_f$ example: a spot moves 3.0 cm while the solvent moves 6.0 cm, so $R_f = 3.0 \div 6.0 = 0.50$.

applications.title: Forensic science
applications.body: Chromatography separates the inks in a forged document or the dyes in a fibre, and $R_f$ values identify them against known samples.

applications.title: Drinking water
applications.body: Water companies test pH and dissolved solids, as you do in practical 8. In the UK they make water safe by filtering and sterilising it. Where fresh water is short, sea water is distilled or forced through membranes, which takes a lot of energy.
